newsitem.title: CHINA: China premier says Japan militarists undermine ties.
newsitem.headline: China premier says Japan militarists undermine ties.

text.p: Chinese Premier Li Peng said on Monday Japanese rightists had undermined Sino-Japanese relations by repairing a lighthouse on a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea, but forecast failure for the ultranationalists.
Chinese Vice Foreign Minister Tang Jiaxuan summoned Japan's ambassador on September 27 and raised the issue of the death of a Hong Kong protest leader, state radio said. It gave no further details.

Anti-Japanese sentiment surged in Hong Kong when activist David Chan drowned last week after jumping off a protest ship in defiance of a Japanese blockade of the islands, known as the Diaoyus in Chinese and as the Senkakus in Japanese.
Hong Kong, currently a British colony, reverts to Chinese rule in mid-1997.

In a speech on the eve of National Day, Premier Li said: "Recently a tiny handful of rightwingers and militarists in Japan have created a series of incidents which have interfered with and undermined Sino-Japanese relations.

"No action that hurts the feeling of the Chinese people will get anywhere," he said in remarks that drew widespread applause from an audience of top officials gathered in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing.
China had achieved significant results by upholding its principles, withstanding pressure and "waging justifiable and restrained struggle" when the time was right, Li said.

China and Japan have been embroiled in a row over the uninhabited islands since September when Japanese rightists moved to buttress Tokyo's claim over them by sailing there and repairing a makeshift aluminium lighthouse.

Both China and Japan are reluctant to strain their relations and are slightly at a loss over how to deal with the two-month-old wave of nationalist passion that has swept Chinese communities in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.

Beijing and Taipei, rivals since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949, agree the Diaoyus have been China's for centuries and dispute Tokyo's claim, which dates to 1895 when Japan defeated imperial China in a war and seized the islands.
Japan has refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion.
Two of China's most prominent dissidents on Monday demanded Beijing get tough with Tokyo by conducting missile tests near the islands.
